name: Kaan Aksit
summary: This project focuses on merging artificial intelligence techniques with physical principles to advance the realism of immersive displays. Situated at the intersection of AI, physics, and display technology, the research aims to develop innovative solutions for tasks such as realistic rendering, haptic feedback, and motion tracking within virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) contexts. Students will leverage high-performance computing, optimization algorithms, and machine learning techniques to design and implement physically informed AI algorithms. The work involves exploring how physical principles can enhance AI models and provides hands-on experience with state-of-the-art hardware and software tools. This interdisciplinary project is suitable for students in UCL's Master's program in Scientific and Data Intensive Computing who are interested in developing skills in AI, high-performance computing, optimization, and data analysis. Through this research, participants will contribute to pushing the boundaries of immersive display technology by creating more engaging and realistic digital experiences using data-driven and physically informed approaches.

name: Timo Betcke
summary: This project addresses the current lack of robust GPU acceleration support within the Rust programming language, which is gaining popularity in scientific computing. The primary objective is to investigate existing GPU computing toolkits available for Rust and explore ways to evolve the language's GPU computing ecosystem. The work involves a hands-on experimental approach, specifically setting up benchmark experiments to evaluate these toolkits. This software-oriented project requires students to analyze performance and investigate development paths for the ecosystem. Interested applicants should have an interest in systems programming and scientific computing. To apply, students must provide a CV and a brief outline of their previous programming experience. Please note that the successful candidate is expected to dedicate substantial time to the project throughout the entire academic year.

name: Nikos Nikolaou
summary: Dr. Nikos Nikolaou offers two distinct research opportunities. The first project focuses on uncertainty estimation and interpretability in medical imaging, aiming to investigate how improving uncertainty quantification affects model explanations and trustworthiness. Students will handle real-world imaging data, training state-of-the-art models like CNNs or ViTs using rigorous methodologies such as data augmentation and imputation. This experimental, data-driven project requires Python proficiency and machine learning experience, ideally in medical applications; it is suitable for students interested in either uncertainty quantification or interpretability. The second project is a more theoretical and algorithmic investigation into alternatives to backpropagation, such as local learning rules, Hebbian updates, and the NoProp framework. This coding-heavy research involves implementing and benchmarking these methods on image classification and sequence modeling tasks while exploring their intersection with network sparsity and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis. Applicants must possess a strong mathematical and algorithmic background alongside experience with deep learning frameworks like PyTorch, TensorFlow, or Keras. Both projects require significant technical expertise in deep learning architectures and optimization.

name: Guido Germano
summary: This software-oriented project aims to improve the performance of QMGA, an open-source C++ molecular graphics program used for the interactive rendering of large ensembles of convex bodies in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The primary scientific objective is to enhance rendering speed and accessibility for datasets that now reach millions of particles. Students can pursue two main development paths. One option focuses on optimizing the existing OpenGL-based C++ codebase by implementing modern techniques such as occlusion queries, backface culling, and vertex buffer objects, while also updating library calls for Linux compatibility and porting the software to macOS and Windows. Alternatively, a student could undertake a significant rewrite of the program using WebGL and JavaScript to create 'WebMGA,' a version designed to work universally without complex build or compatibility issues. Tasks include updating makefiles, migrating distribution to GitHub, and modifying source code for performance. This project is ideal for students interested in computer graphics, high-performance rendering, and cross-platform software development.

name: Mose Giordano
summary: This software-oriented project focuses on developing a high-performance implementation of an algorithm based on the non-equispaced fast Fourier transform within the Julia programming language. Situated in the domain of Astronomy, the work aims to enhance the LombScargle.jl open-source package, which utilizes the Lomb-Scargle periodogram to detect periods in unevenly sampled signals, such as variable star light curves. The student will implement this new algorithm and conduct performance comparisons against existing implementations found in the current package. The primary objective is to deliver a more efficient computational method for scientific computing. This project is highly coding-intensive and involves contributing directly to an active Julia-based scientific library. While specific prerequisites are not explicitly listed, the work requires familiarity with high-level programming for scientific computing and algorithm implementation. The project is ideal for students interested in high-performance computing, numerical algorithms, and astronomical data processing tools.

name: Peter Bentley
summary: Two distinct research projects are available under the supervision of Peter Bentley. The first, 'Deep Morphogenesis', aims to develop a distributed generative design process that mimics biological development to create complex 3D forms. This project involves combining machine learning models like GANs or VAEs with cellular automata or multi-agent systems, using techniques such as genetic algorithms or novelty search to explore representations that are expressive and adaptable to environments. The second project, 'Evolving Latent Variables', focuses on optimizing search spaces by using generative ML to learn smooth, searchable latent representations from existing solutions. Students will investigate how GANs and VAEs compare in their ability to enable effective optimization via genetic algorithms in complex, multi-objective, or constrained real-world problems. Both projects are research-oriented and involve building new models or investigating generative approaches. For the first project, Python programming is essential, and experience with machine learning or evolutionary computation is useful. These projects are ideal for students interested in the intersection of deep learning, evolutionary computation, and generative design.

name: Edina Rosta
summary: Edina Rosta supervises several interdisciplinary projects at the intersection of machine learning and molecular biophysics. One project focuses on using autoencoders to identify latent space for protein dynamics by analyzing MD simulation trajectories. Another explores combining ML with MD simulations to develop Machine Learning Transition State Analysis (MLTSA) for identifying relevant variables in protein unbinding processes. A third project advances a reinforcement learning framework, specifically PPO/SAC, to accelerate rare events in molecular simulations through autonomous bias placement. A fourth project investigates algorithms to bias sampling on kinetic networks using stochastic block models and Monte Carlo methods. A fifth project uses bioinformatics and ML to classify NTP-processing enzymes by connecting protein sequences to biochemical functions. Finally, one project applies causal inference algorithms like PCMCI and Transfer Entropy to identify directional relationships in complex time-series data from MD simulations. These projects are highly coding-intensive and data-driven, requiring proficiency in Python and familiarity with ML frameworks like TensorFlow or PyTorch. Students interested in computational chemistry, structural biology, or advanced statistical modeling will find these suitable.

name: Kris Thielemans
summary: Kris Thielemans offers four distinct research projects focused on improving quantitative accuracy in PET and SPECT imaging. One project investigates adapting partial volume correction (PVC) methods to the lung using Python and SIRF software, involving realistic image simulation and potential 3D printed object scanning. A second project explores a novel deep learning approach using CNNs to estimate average PET sensitivity for motion correction in the thorax. The third project focuses on using machine learning techniques, such as U-Net architectures, to denoise SPECT images to improve quantitative accuracy in small volumes of interest. Finally, a fourth project evaluates energy-based scatter correction methods in PET using STIR software, comparing PDF calculation approaches like the Method of Moments against traditional Single Scatter Simulation. These projects are primarily coding-heavy and data-driven, requiring programming experience in Python or MATLAB. While basic knowledge of CNNs or PET is helpful, it is not always required. Students interested in medical imaging, quantitative analysis, and making meaningful research contributions will find these projects suitable.

name: Michael Parkes
summary: This software-oriented project aims to develop a programme for analysing 3D Background Orientated Schlieren (BOS) images to examine density changes in materials. The primary objective is to create code capable of processing various image formats, including JPEG, TIF, and PNG, as well as movie frames like MPEG and AVI, to apply the BOS method. A key component involves processing data from a plenoptic camera by setting different depths of field and focal points to generate computer-generated focused images. The student will implement methods to generate BOS backgrounds using techniques such as wavelet or Pellin noise and produce both BOS images and velocity fields. By coupling BOS with plenoptic camera data, the project seeks to achieve a 3D understanding of chemical and physical changes, such as concentration gradients in water and alcohol mixing. This work involves handling large numbers of files and performing complicated analysis procedures. The project is highly coding-heavy, focusing on computational processing to detect minute differences between images for density change visualization.

name: Gopinathan Sankar
summary: This project focuses on the analysis of data derived from Synchrotron Radiation based X-ray techniques. The primary objective involves investigating and processing complex datasets produced by these advanced X-ray methods. The work is centered within the scientific context of synchrotron radiation research, requiring a focus on the interpretation of specialized experimental outputs. Students will engage in the analytical aspects of handling data generated through these high-energy radiation techniques. Given the emphasis on data analysis, the project involves investigating patterns and features within the provided X-ray datasets. The nature of the work is fundamentally data-driven, centered on the computational or mathematical processing of synchrotron-based measurements. There are no specific prerequisites or student background requirements explicitly stated in the project description. This opportunity is suitable for students interested in the intersection of X-ray physics and data science. It would be less appropriate for those seeking purely theoretical physics research without a focus on experimental data analysis.

name: Ben Waugh
summary: This supervisor offers three distinct projects within the field of particle physics software development. The first project focuses on refactoring the Atlantis Java application, an event display for LHC proton collisions, to improve its testability and extensibility; this requires knowledge of object-oriented design, with experience in Java and design patterns being advantageous. The second project involves enhancing the YODA C++ library by introducing full chi-squared support using the Eigen library and modernising its interface with the Contur tool, making it ideal for students interested in high-performance C++ development and applied statistics. The third project explores applying machine learning techniques, such as active learning, to the Python-based Contur toolkit to more efficiently test Beyond the Standard Model theories by optimizing parameter space scanning. This research-oriented task involves investigating how ML can enhance model consistency testing against LHC data. These projects range from software-oriented refactoring and C++ library enhancement to data-driven machine learning investigations within scientific computing.

name: Frank Smith
summary: This project involves investigating fluid flows through a branching vessel to determine how much throughput is possible as the number of branches increases. The research will be conducted using a combination of modelling, analysis, and computation, focusing on high flow rates within two spatial dimensions at the outset. While the background motivation for this work is biomedical, the study also encompasses several industrial applications. Students will engage in a computational and analytical approach to address the core question of throughput capacity in branching structures. The project requires an interest in fluid dynamics and the application of mathematical modelling to physical systems. There are no specific prerequisites explicitly stated beyond the technical scope of the investigation itself. This work is suitable for students interested in the intersection of fluid mechanics, computation, and biological or industrial flow problems.

name: Anthony Lynas-Gray
summary: This supervisor offers two distinct computational projects in astrophysics. The first project focuses on time-frequency analysis of interrupted light curves, specifically investigating the photometry of V2076 Oph. Students will implement the time-frequency analysis method developed by Jorge et al. (2006) using Wavelet Packet and Local Sine Packet Transforms to handle non-sinusoidal or time-dependent variations that standard Fourier transforms cannot model. The second project addresses uncertainties in gravitational light deflection predictions for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA). This software-oriented task involves writing a program to reproduce the maximum gravitational deflection predictions from Li et al. (2022) and incorporating properly calculated error bars based on the Gravitational Constant (G). The student will then assess the prospects for a new determination of G by comparing measured and observed deflections of light from objects outside the Solar System. Both projects are highly technical and involve implementing specific algorithms and models to analyze astronomical data or predict physical phenomena within the context of radio astronomy and stellar photometry.

name: Gabriel Facini
summary: This supervisor offers two distinct research directions at the interface of AI and experimental particle physics within the ATLAS collaboration. The first project focuses on applying transformer architectures to Higgs boson tagging at the energy frontier, specifically identifying Higgs bosons decaying into two b-quarks in extreme kinematic regimes. This work involves developing models, addressing model explainability through XAI techniques, and evaluating performance on ATLAS Run 3 collision data using Python and ATLAS software frameworks. The second project explores Large Language Models (LLMs) to transform how physicists interact with distributed scientific knowledge. Students may implement advanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques, explore GraphRAG, or fine-tune LLMs and embedding models to develop a custom chatbot for querying complex documentation. Both projects are highly practical and data-driven, offering experience in deep learning, natural language processing, and large-scale data analysis. While no explicit prerequisites are listed, the work requires a willingness to work independently and an interest in applying modern machine learning architectures to fundamental physics problems.

name: Kjell Erlandsson
summary: This project investigates the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to correct parametric images for motion in dynamic Positron Emission Tomography (PET). In dynamic PET, radiotracer distribution is measured over time to investigate metabolic processes via kinetic modelling; however, patient motion during long scans can dramatically impact the resulting parametric images. The objective is to explore a novel approach using CNNs to address these motion effects, which differs from traditional blind deconvolution methods used for blurring removal. This research-oriented project involves investigating deep learning architectures to achieve motion correction and holds potential for publication. Essential prerequisites include programming experience, ideally in Python or MATLAB. While not strictly required, basic knowledge of CNN architectures for imaging and training is desired. The ideal candidate should possess a strong interest in making meaningful contributions to research. The work focuses on applying deep learning techniques to medical imaging reconstruction to improve the accuracy of metabolic process investigations in vivo.

name: Mark Buitelaar
summary: This project aims to develop machine learning algorithms to automate the tuning of double quantum dot devices, addressing the formidable task of managing large numbers of gate electrodes in large-scale quantum computing architectures. Set within the context of solid-state charge or spin qubits, the research focuses on using carbon nanotube double quantum dots as building blocks for encoding quantum information. The student will develop and test machine learning algorithms using large datasets acquired from ultraclean carbon nanotube devices measured in a mK dilution refrigerator via radio-frequency reflectometry readout. As the application of machine learning is a new development in this lab, the work will likely involve significant trial-and-error. This project is suitable for students with a strong interest in quantum physics, solid-state physics, and computer science. Essential prerequisites include experience with machine learning techniques. The work involves both algorithmic development and experimental testing using optimized data acquisition systems.

name: Michel Tsamados
summary: This project aims to expand upon the ARISGAN software, which previously achieved 30x super-resolution of Sentinel-3 OLCI optical imagery. The primary objective is to adapt this Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) approach to achieve 5x super-resolution, specifically transforming Sentinel-1 microwave imager data (50m resolution) to the resolution of Sentinel-2 optical images (10m resolution). The research is situated within the domain of Arctic sea ice monitoring, with potential real-world applications for supporting safe travel for an Inuit Social enterprise in Pond Inlet. By leveraging the ability of Sentinel-1 microwave sensors to see through clouds and darkness, the project explores the possibility of synthesizing artificial 'daylight' imagery at super-resolution during nighttime or cloudy conditions. The student will build upon existing software to implement and test this new super-resolution approach for microwave frequencies. This data-driven project focuses on adapting established GAN architectures to a different sensor modality and resolution scale within the context of remote sensing and satellite imagery synthesis.

name: Marta Betcke
summary: Marta Betcke offers several research opportunities focusing on the intersection of machine learning and computational physics. One project explores learning correction for long steps in pseudo-spectral methods for solving the wave equation, while another investigates learned parallel in-time integration of dynamical systems. Research into neural operators is available for solving oscillatory problems such as the Helmholtz, Wave, and Westervelt equations. Other topics include using weakly convex neural networks for inverse problem regularisation and employing diffusion models as priors for inverse problem solutions. In the domain of medical imaging, projects involve developing photoacoustic image reconstruction methods—potentially learning optimal acquisition protocols or time-dependent regularisers—and building an image reconstruction platform for ultrasound tomography. This software engineering-focused project requires setting up a flexible platform capable of interfacing with different forward solvers and inversion methods. These projects range from theoretical and data-driven investigations to heavy research software engineering, making them suitable for students interested in deep learning, numerical analysis, and computational imaging.

name: Franca Fraternali
summary: Two distinct research projects are available under the supervision of Franca Fraternali. The first project focuses on protein engineering using Transformer-based models to perform in-silico sequence evolution across various protein families. The student will investigate potential model biases by running state-of-the-art Transformers, exploring generated sequences, and using libraries like NumPy and SciPy to analyze changes in model embeddings. This data-driven project requires strong Python programming skills and knowledge of Machine Learning. The second project addresses hit-to-lead drug discovery by integrating Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with Machine Learning to optimize chemical structures. The objective is to use ML algorithms to suggest compounds for binding free energy estimation via MD, thereby improving screening efficiency. This project involves light coding for simulation management and result analysis using embedding similarity. While the first project is specifically suited for students with a background in ML and Python, both projects involve computational modeling and analyzing complex datasets to improve predictive accuracy in bioinformatics and drug development.

name: Jamie Dean
summary: This project aims to address the challenge of radiation-induced neurocognitive side effects in paediatric central nervous system tumours by identifying which brain regions are most sensitive to radiotherapy. Using a dataset from mice treated with proton beam radiotherapy, the research involves analysing spatial maps of radiotherapy dose, digital histology images, and molecular sequencing data quantifying gene activity across different cell types. The student will perform multimodal data integration by mapping these diverse datasets onto a single spatial coordinate system defined by a brain atlas. Key tasks include segmenting cells and labelling identities using state-of-the-art machine learning models, measuring differences in cell type abundance and shape, and performing statistical analyses to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying differential cellular responses. This data-driven project offers experience in applying data integration, machine learning, and statistical analysis methods to a high-priority biomedical problem. No prior knowledge of biology or medicine is necessary, making it suitable for students interested in applying advanced computational techniques to complex biological datasets.

name: Nora Yitong Qiu
summary: Nora Yitong Qiu offers two distinct research opportunities. The first project focuses on improving Optical Character Recognition (OCR) accuracy for premodern East Asian scripts, such as Manchu documents and Chinese calligraphy, by developing AI and machine learning techniques to overcome challenges like brushwork variability and archival degradation. Students may train models on annotated corpora to enable large-scale textual analysis in Qing or late imperial studies; this project is suitable for those with technical backgrounds or interests in digital humanities and historical linguistics. The second project employs social network analysis, regression modeling, and longue durée historical comparison using the China Biographical Database (CBDB) to examine the evolution of elite political networks in imperial China. Students will investigate how kinship, patronage, and examination ties shaped bureaucratic hierarchies and how dynastic transitions or ethnicity influenced elite structures across regimes like the Tang, Yuan, or Qing. This research-driven project explores the sociological dynamics of power and authority within historical Chinese political networks.

name: Adam Gibson
summary: This project aims to develop a data-driven, AI-assisted system to automate the collation of early modern printed books. In the field of digital humanities, scholars traditionally identify text differences between copies manually, a process that is slow and error-prone due to stop-press corrections. Working with a large dataset of digitized pages, you will implement image processing and machine learning techniques to identify subtle variations between digitized images. Key technical challenges include handling page curvature, warping, bleed-through, and aligning images from different digitization systems, while distinguishing printed text from annotations. You will develop algorithms for preprocessing, registration, variant detection, and classification, potentially exploring pixel-based comparison alternatives to OCR or using supervised learning and unsupervised clustering. Additionally, you will consider the design of a user interface to display results to scholars. This open-ended project is suitable for students interested in problem-solving and applying AI to historical or cultural data.

name: Jon Butterworth
summary: This software-oriented project focuses on optimizing the Contur toolkit, a Python-based tool used in particle physics to test Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) theories against CERN Large Hadron Collider data. The research problem involves addressing the high computational cost and time-consuming nature of analyzing large grids of model predictions when varying multiple parameters. To improve efficiency, the student will work on optimizing both the Python code and the existing relational database design used to store models, grids, parameters, exclusions, and histograms. Specific tasks include benchmarking and profiling Python code, analyzing database queries, and implementing and testing performance-improving techniques. The project is highly technical and involves software optimization within a computational physics context. Successful candidates should possess familiarity with the UNIX shell, Python, SQL and database technologies, and git. This project is ideal for students interested in high-performance computing, database optimization, and scientific software engineering, rather than those seeking purely theoretical or experimental physics research.

name: Maxim Molodsov
summary: This project investigates the fundamental biological problem of how cells achieve extreme DNA compaction while maintaining accessibility for reading, copying, and repairing genes. The research focuses on understanding the integration of two distinct organizational mechanisms: liquid-like condensates formed by multivalent interactions between nucleosomes and loop extrusion driven by the molecular machine condensin. Using the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulator, the student will test how these two mechanisms work together mechanistically. This computational project is designed for a student with a strong interest in biology and good modelling experience. The work involves using simulation tools to investigate the interplay between physical interactions and active loop-forming processes. By modeling these molecular building blocks, the project aims to clarify how large-scale genomic organization emerges from individual mechanical actions. The study sits at the intersection of biophysics and computational modeling, requiring a focus on mechanistic integration through molecular dynamics.

name: Jonathan Tennyson
summary: Jonathan Tennyson offers four distinct research opportunities ranging from database construction to workflow automation. One project involves constructing a new cooling functions database for the ExoMol website using existing data to model processes from the early universe to planetary atmospheres. Another software-oriented project focuses on adding highly charged atomic line lists to the ExoAtoms database by capturing and formatting external data into standard ExoMol format; students may find the Information Retrieval and Data Mining course helpful. A third project is a data-driven investigation into determining the approximate ages of exoplanets by matching planets from known catalogues with available host star age data. Finally, a more automation-focused project aims to design a complete workflow for running MARVEL using data provided by large language models, building on previous work to make the determination of molecular energy levels quicker and less labour intensive. These projects primarily involve data retrieval, formatting, and workflow development within the context of molecular spectroscopy and astrophysics.

name: Nikos Konstantinidis
summary: This project investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably assess MSci/MSc project reports when provided with an explicit marking rubric and assessment criteria. The research aims to compare grades and criterion-level judgments from several publicly accessible LLMs against those assigned by human academic markers using a corpus of previously graded reports. Through this comparative approach, the study will quantify agreement levels and identify which models align most closely with human judgment. Additionally, the work will test whether LLM outputs can improve inter-marker consistency via rubric-based calibration or function as a third cross-check during instances of disagreement between human markers. The project involves an experimental and data-driven investigation into the utility of LLMs for automated assessment tasks. Students will focus on analyzing model performance and evaluating the reliability of LLM-generated feedback against established academic standards. This research is centered on the application of large language models within the context of academic grading and assessment consistency.

name: William Woof
summary: Two distinct projects are available focusing on deep learning applications for retinal imaging and rare eye diseases. The first project, Vision-language fusion for rare eye diseases, addresses the limitation of small, unstructured datasets in diagnosing rare ocular conditions. It investigates how foundation language models and vision-language models can bootstrap small datasets by utilizing natural language instructions from expert ophthalmologists, focusing on fine-tuning off-the-shelf models rather than training new ones from scratch. The second project, EyeNomaly, explores anomaly detection using deep unsupervised learning. Building upon the Eye2Gene algorithm for identifying Inherited Retinal Dystrophies (IRDs), this work utilizes a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) trained to generate retinal scans. The objective is to adapt these GANs for anomaly detection to flag potential eye disorders by identifying deviations from healthy patient data. This project is particularly suited for students interested in deep unsupervised learning and the application of generative models to medical imaging tasks.

name: Tony Lynas-Gray
summary: This supervisor offers three distinct computational projects. The first focuses on software development, requiring students to set up the NEMESISPY retrieval code and write a program to generate opacity tables for specific molecules using ExoMol database data. The second project is more algorithm-oriented, involving the creation of an opacity distribution function (ODF) representation from monochromatic opacities; students will implement programs for ODF calculation and one-dimensional radiative transfer to optimize bin-size. The third project is a physics-based programming task centered on General Relativity, where the objective is to develop a computer program that calculates necessary time corrections for astronomical observations made on the lunar surface relative to the Solar System Barycentre. All three projects are coding-heavy and involve numerical implementation. Prerequisites include specific readings (Yang et al. 2024, Cernetic et al. 2019, or Ashby & Patla 2024) and the High Performance Computing module is recommended for all. These projects are ideal for students interested in computational astrophysics, molecular spectroscopy, or relativistic physics.

name: Sergey Yurchenko
summary: This software-oriented project aims to design and implement the ExoMol Opacity App, a web interface designed to address computational bottlenecks in exoplanetary spectroscopy. While the ExoMol project provides essential high-temperature molecular data for modelling exoplanet atmospheres—crucial for interpreting observations from the James Webb Space Telescope and the ESA Ariel mission—current pre-computed opacity tables cannot capture the full diversity of discovered exoplanets. The student will develop a system that allows atmospheric modellers to configure custom opacity requests by selecting specific spectral ranges, resolutions, temperatures, pressures, and compositions. This work involves building an interface capable of submitting these requests to high-performance computing (HPC) resources and retrieving tailored results. Consequently, the project combines web development, HPC job scheduling, and large-scale data handling. The implementation will directly empower the global astronomy community by enabling customized atmospheric retrievals. This project is ideal for students interested in software engineering, web development, and managing complex computational workflows involving high-performance computing and large datasets.

name: Federico Galvanin
summary: This project aims to develop a digital twin for liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) systems used in the recovery of precious metals within continuous flow small channels. The research focuses on modeling segmented flow, where two immiscible liquids move in repeating patterns of slugs and plugs. To achieve this, the student will implement a joint system identification framework that combines data-driven modeling for hydrodynamics with physics-based first principles for mass transfer. Specifically, the work involves applying model-based design of experiments (MBDoE) methods and active learning to identify both the machine learning and physical components of a hybrid segmented flow model. The resulting digital twin will be utilized for LLE process simulation and scenario-based optimization. This project is highly interdisciplinary, blending chemical engineering principles with advanced computational techniques such as machine learning and mathematical modeling. It is suitable for students interested in digital technologies, hybrid modeling, and the development of mathematical models that interact continuously with physical systems to optimize process quality.

name: Siyin Liu
summary: This project aims to develop and validate a state-of-the-art deep learning pipeline for the automated, quantitative analysis of In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM) images to discover novel digital biomarkers for Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD). Using a unique longitudinal dataset from the FECD-TRACE cohort, the research addresses the clinical need for sensitive imaging endpoints in early disease stages. The student will undertake a data-driven project involving data pre-processing, model training, and rigorous validation. Depending on their specific interests, tasks may include developing robust classifiers for image quality control, building sophisticated segmentation models to quantify cellular pathology, or exploring self-supervised learning with Vision Transformers, such as DINO, for representation learning. The work involves tackling complex computer vision challenges to link discovered features to curated clinical and genetic data. This project is suitable for students interested in medical imaging, deep learning, and the application of artificial intelligence to ophthalmology. The core responsibilities involve implementing end-to-end pipelines to transform high-resolution, complex IVCM datasets into actionable clinical insights.
